WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Louisiana Gov. Bobby Jindal is set to deliver the Republican response to President Obama's upcoming joint address to Congress, a high-profile slot the party often gives to one of its rising stars. Louisiana Gov. Bobby Jindal, 37, will give GOP response to President Obama's address to Congress this month. "Gov. Jindal embodies what I have long said: The Republican Party must not be simply the party of 'opposition,' but the party of better solutions," House Minority Leader John Boehner said in a Wednesday statement. Jindal, a former congressman in his first term as Louisiana's governor, was widely believed to be on Republican presidential nominee John McCain's short list for vice president, and he often served as a campaign surrogate on the Arizona senator's behalf. The 37-year-old son of Indian immigrants also was given a prime-time speaking slot at the GOP convention last September, though he ultimately decided not to attend the four-day event as Hurricane Gustav headed for landfall in his state. An Ivy League grad and Rhodes Scholar, and his state's first nonwhite governor, Jindal has long been on the GOP's radar screen as a potential future leader and likely presidential candidate. And as the GOP is launching full-scale efforts to appeal to nonwhite voters, Jindal has become one of the party's most high-profile minorities. "His stewardship of the state of Louisiana, dedication to reforming government and commitment to bringing forth new and innovative ideas make him a leader not just within the Republican Party, but in our nation as a whole," Boehner also said of Jindal on Wednesday. Jindal, who became governor two years after Hurricane Katrina ravaged Louisiana, has drawn praise for spearheading the ongoing recovery efforts. "When you look at major statewide offices Republicans have won over the past three years, there is one, Louisiana," said Alex Castellanos, a CNN contributor and Republican strategist. "In a state where we lost confidence in government, perhaps more than any other state, he restored it and cut taxes." Though he is often mentioned as a likely contender for the 2012 Republican presidential race, Jindal has said his current focus is on winning reelection in 2011. Jindal also said late last year that even if he were considering running for president, now is the time to support the sitting president. "It doesn't matter whether you're Republican, Democrat or independent, it doesn't matter whether you voted for him or not, President-elect Barack Obama is our president," he said. The White House announced on Tuesday that Obama will deliver the annual State of the Union address to both houses of Congress on February 24. In 2008, Democrats tapped Kansas Gov. Kathleen Sebelius -- then considered to be a possible vice presidential candidate -- to give the rebuttal speech to former President Bush's final State of the Union address. Other Democrats who delivered responses to Bush's State of the Unions include Virginia Sen. Jim Webb, Virginia Gov. Tim Kaine, and former Washington Gov. Gary Locke, the nation's first Chinese-American governor. The last Republican to deliver a response to a State of the Union address was Maine Sen. Susan Collins in 2000.

The response to a presidential address to Congress is a coveted, if often thankless, opportunity. Delivered without the pomp, the cheering crowds, or the historic backdrop that the president enjoys, respondents speak from a bare room or empty studio, addressing a much smaller television audience. Yet the assignment has historically served as a launching pad, or at least a signal of confidence, for rising stars within the party out of power. Previous responders have included governors and senators whom party leaders hoped might embody a fresher, more compelling alternative to the sitting president's message.

That contrast is not incidental. In the aftermath of the 2008 election, Republican strategists and officials have been engaged in a broader conversation about how to expand the party's appeal beyond its traditional base, particularly among nonwhite and younger voters who broke heavily for Obama and the Democrats. Jindal's ascension to this high-profile role is widely seen as part of that effort—an implicit answer to the question of who might help the GOP look and sound different in the years ahead.

**WASHINGTON** — When Governor Bobby Jindal takes the podium tonight to deliver the Republican response to President Obama's address to Congress, he will do so as arguably the most closely watched rising star in a party desperately searching for new leadership and direction.

The 37-year-old Louisiana governor's selection for this high-profile role has fueled speculation that GOP strategists are positioning him as a potential standard-bearer for the party's future — possibly as soon as 2012.

## A Rapid Ascent

Jindal's political trajectory has been extraordinary by any measure. The son of Indian immigrants, he served as Louisiana's health secretary before winning a congressional seat in 2004. In 2007, he was elected governor at just 36, becoming the nation's youngest sitting governor and the first Indian-American to hold that office.

"Bobby represents everything our party needs right now — he's young, he's smart, he's got real executive experience, and he's not afraid to make tough calls," said one senior Republican National Committee official who requested anonymity to speak candidly about internal party strategy. "After the drubbing we took in November, we need fresh faces who can articulate conservative principles in a way that resonates beyond our traditional base."

Republican pollster Whit Ayres was more direct in his assessment: "Jindal checks boxes that matter enormously for a party trying to rebuild. He's a policy wonk who can talk healthcare and budgets fluently, but he also has a compelling personal story. In a party sometimes criticized for lacking diversity, he offers a very different face."

## The Response Speech

Party leaders describe tonight's response as both an opportunity and a test. Jindal will need to offer substantive conservative alternatives to Obama's economic agenda while introducing himself to a national audience that, despite his gubernatorial win, remains largely unfamiliar with him.

"This is his coming-out party on the national stage," said Republican strategist Mary Matalin. "The pressure is real, but so is the opportunity. If he delivers, people will start seriously talking about him in a different context."

House Minority Leader John Boehner, who was involved in selecting Jindal for the response, praised the governor's credentials. "Bobby has been a reformer his entire career. He inherited a state dealing with the aftermath of Katrina and corruption, and he's brought real change. That's the kind of leadership story Americans want to hear right now."

## 2012 Speculation

While Jindal himself has consistently downplayed presidential ambitions — telling reporters as recently as last week that he's "focused entirely on Louisiana" — the speculation persists, driven largely by operatives eager to identify next-generation leaders.

"Nobody serious is measuring drapes for the Oval Office right now," cautioned one veteran GOP consultant. "But smart people are watching him closely. If this speech goes well, and if he continues delivering results in Louisiana, his name will absolutely be part of the 2012 conversation, whether he encourages it publicly or not."

Some conservative commentators have already begun drawing comparisons to other young governors who used national moments to launch broader ambitions.

"Every generation, the party looks for someone who can bridge the establishment and the grassroots, someone who excites both the base and independents," said conservative radio host and commentator Laura Ingraham. "Jindal has that potential, but potential isn't the same as delivering. Tonight matters."

## Skepticism Remains

Not everyone is convinced the hype is warranted. Some Democratic strategists and even a few Republican voices caution against premature crowning.

"Responding to a State of the Union address has been a graveyard for political ambitions as often as a launching pad," noted one Democratic communications strategist, pointing to past responses that failed to resonate or were overshadowed by production issues.

Others within the GOP worry about placing outsized expectations on any single figure so early in a rebuilding process. "We need a bench, not a savior," said one House Republican aide. "Bobby's talented, no doubt. But let's not put the entire party's hopes on one 30-minute speech."

## Looking Ahead

Regardless of how tonight's speech is received, Jindal's re-election prospects in Louisiana next year and his handling of the state's budget challenges will likely factor heavily into any future national ambitions. Louisiana, like most states, faces significant fiscal pressure amid the broader economic downturn, and Jindal's responses to federal stimulus funds have already drawn both praise and criticism from within his own party.

For now, Republican leaders seem content to let the moment build organically. As one senior party strategist put it: "Let's see what happens tonight. Political stars are made and unmade by single speeches all the time. But the raw material is clearly there."

Whether tonight marks the beginning of a national political ascent or simply a notable moment in a promising gubernatorial career remains to be seen. What is clear is that, for one night at least, the eyes of the political world will be on Baton Rouge's young governor as he attempts to offer a compelling vision for a party still searching for its footing after a difficult election cycle.
